questions.q: What does third normal form (3NF) remove from a relational model?
options: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
Transitive dependencies, where a non-key column depends on another non-key column
questions.explain: 1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF removes partial dependencies, and 3NF removes transitive dependencies.

questions.q: In a star schema, what does a fact table usually hold?
options: Descriptive attributes such as customer names
Measurements of business events, with keys to the dimension tables
questions.explain: Facts are the measurable events (a repair, a payment). Dimensions describe them (who, what, where, when).

questions.q: How does a Type 2 slowly changing dimension handle a change, such as a tenant moving address?
options: It adds a new row with effective dates, keeping the old row as history
It adds a new column for the previous value
questions.explain: Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 adds a new versioned row, Type 3 keeps a limited previous value in a column.

questions.q: Which level of data model shows the main business concepts and how they relate, without technical detail?
questions.explain: Conceptual models describe business concepts. Logical models add attributes and keys. Physical models add database specifics.

questions.q: What is a surrogate key?
options: A key made from several business columns
A system-generated identifier with no business meaning
A key that points to another table
questions.explain: Surrogate keys stay stable even when business identifiers change or clash across sources.

questions.q: What's the main difference between a data lake and a data warehouse?
options: A lake holds raw data in many formats, with structure applied when it's read. A warehouse holds modelled, structured data
questions.explain: Lakes use schema on read; warehouses use schema on write. Lakehouses combine elements of both.

questions.q: What does data lineage describe?
options: Who is allowed to see data
Where data came from and how it moved and changed along the way
questions.explain: Lineage helps with trust, impact analysis and debugging when numbers look wrong.

questions.q: In a data mesh, who owns data products?
options: The domain teams closest to the data
questions.explain: Data mesh treats data as a product owned by domains, on a shared self-serve platform with federated governance.

questions.q: What is master data management for?
options: Creating one trusted version of core entities, such as people, properties or products
questions.explain: MDM matches and merges records from different systems so everyone uses the same core entities.

questions.q: Metadata is best described as:
options: Data about data, such as definitions, owners, formats and lineage
questions.explain: Good metadata makes data findable, understandable and trustworthy.

questions.q: Which of these is a lawful basis for processing personal data under UK GDPR?
options: The data is already in a spreadsheet
The data is more than a year old
questions.explain: The six lawful bases are consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.

questions.q: When do you need a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
options: Only when a breach has happened
When processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals
questions.explain: DPIAs are required for high-risk processing, such as large-scale use of special category data or new technologies.

questions.q: What does data minimisation mean?
options: Collecting and keeping only the personal data you need for your purpose
Deleting all data after a month
questions.explain: It's one of the UK GDPR principles, alongside purpose limitation and storage limitation.

questions.q: Which of these is a data quality dimension in the Government Data Quality Framework?
questions.explain: The six dimensions are accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and validity.

questions.q: What is a data steward usually responsible for?
options: The day-to-day quality, definitions and correct use of a set of data
Physical security of the data centre
questions.explain: Stewards look after data on behalf of the data owner, who stays accountable.

questions.q: How is ELT different from ETL?
options: ELT loads raw data into the target first, then transforms it there
questions.explain: ELT uses the power of modern warehouses to transform after loading, often with tools like dbt.

questions.q: What makes a data pipeline idempotent?
options: Running it more than once with the same input gives the same result
It only runs once a day
questions.explain: Idempotent pipelines can be safely re-run after a failure without creating duplicates.

questions.q: What does change data capture (CDC) do?
options: Identifies changes in source data so only those changes are moved
questions.explain: CDC reduces load and latency compared with copying whole tables every time.

questions.q: Why partition a very large table by date?
options: So queries that filter by date only read the partitions they need
questions.explain: Partition pruning cuts the amount of data scanned, which saves time and cost.

questions.q: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation?
questions.explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the grouped results.

questions.q: A dataset of rent arrears has a few very large values. Which average is least affected by them?
questions.explain: The median is robust to outliers; the mean gets pulled towards them.

questions.q: Two measures move together strongly. What can you conclude?
options: They are correlated, but that alone doesn't show causation
questions.explain: Correlation needs further evidence, such as an experiment or a clear mechanism, before claiming cause.

questions.q: What is data profiling?
options: Examining source data to understand its structure, content and quality
questions.explain: Profiling finds nulls, outliers, formats and duplicates before you rely on the data.

questions.q: Which chart best shows how a measure changes over months?
questions.explain: Line charts show trends over time clearly.

questions.q: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
options: Only rows that match in both tables
All rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table
Only rows from the right table
questions.explain: Unmatched rows from the right table appear as nulls.

questions.q: In the test pyramid, which kind of test should you have the most of?
questions.explain: Unit tests are fast and cheap, so they form the wide base. End-to-end tests sit at the narrow top.

questions.q: What is regression testing for?
options: Testing a brand new feature for the first time
Checking that recent changes haven't broken existing behaviour
questions.explain: Automated regression suites give teams confidence to release often.

questions.q: A field accepts whole numbers from 1 to 100. Which values does boundary value analysis focus on?
questions.explain: Defects cluster at the edges, so you test on and either side of each boundary.

questions.q: Which of these is non-functional testing?
options: Checking the submit button saves a form
questions.explain: Non-functional testing covers qualities such as performance, security and accessibility.

questions.q: What's the difference between verification and validation?
options: Verification checks we built it right (to spec). Validation checks we built the right thing (for users)
questions.explain: Both matter: a product can meet the spec and still fail its users.

questions.q: In the GOV.UK service lifecycle, which phase comes after discovery?
questions.explain: The phases are discovery, alpha, beta and live.

questions.q: What is a retrospective for?
options: The team looking at how it worked and agreeing improvements
questions.explain: Retros are how teams inspect and adapt their ways of working.

questions.q: Why use work-in-progress (WIP) limits in Kanban?
options: To limit how much is in progress at once, improving flow and exposing bottlenecks
questions.explain: Finishing work before starting more reduces context switching and cycle time.

questions.q: In Scrum, who is accountable for ordering the product backlog to maximise value?
questions.explain: The Product Owner owns the backlog and its order.

questions.q: What is a team's velocity best used for?
options: The team's own planning and forecasting
questions.explain: Velocity is team-specific; comparing teams with it creates bad incentives.

questions.q: What does burn rate describe on a project?
options: The pace at which budget is being spent over time
questions.explain: Tracking burn against plan shows early whether you'll overspend.

questions.q: How is a time and materials contract different from fixed price?
options: Time and materials charges for time actually spent. Fixed price agrees a total for a defined scope
Time and materials is always cheaper
questions.explain: Each shifts risk differently between client and supplier.

questions.q: What does a RAID log track?
options: Risks, assumptions (or actions), issues and dependencies
questions.explain: RAID logs keep the things that could derail delivery visible.

questions.q: What is contingency?
options: Budget or time held back for identified risks
questions.explain: Contingency is sized from risks and released as they're managed.

questions.q: In a consultancy, what does utilisation measure?
options: The share of available time spent on billable work
questions.explain: Utilisation affects the sustainability of the business, alongside day rates.

questions.q: What's the difference between an output and an outcome?
options: An output is something delivered. An outcome is the change it creates for users or the organisation
questions.explain: Teams should measure success by outcomes, not by features shipped.

questions.q: What is a minimum viable product for?
options: Learning whether an idea works with real users, for the least effort
questions.explain: An MVP tests a hypothesis; it isn't a cheap version of the whole product.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the GOV.UK recommended measures for a service?
questions.explain: The four suggested measures are cost per transaction, user satisfaction, completion rate and digital take-up.

questions.q: In MoSCoW prioritisation, what does the W stand for?
questions.explain: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time).

questions.q: What is benefits realisation?
options: Tracking whether expected benefits actually happen after delivery, and acting if not
questions.explain: Benefits are often realised after launch, so ownership needs to continue.

questions.q: Which format is commonly used for user stories?
options: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason]
questions.explain: Given, when, then is often used for acceptance criteria rather than the story itself.

questions.q: What is BPMN used for?
questions.explain: Business Process Model and Notation is a standard way to draw process flows.

questions.q: Which technique helps find the root cause of a problem?
questions.explain: Asking why repeatedly moves you from symptoms to causes.

questions.q: What do acceptance criteria describe?
options: The conditions a story must meet to be accepted as done
questions.explain: Clear criteria reduce rework and help testers.

questions.q: What is as-is and to-be modelling?
options: Mapping how a process works now and how it should work after the change
questions.explain: The gap between them shows what needs to change.

questions.q: What is the minimum contrast ratio for normal body text under WCAG level AA?
questions.explain: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text. 7:1 is the AAA level.

questions.q: Which standard must UK public sector websites meet?
questions.explain: The Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations require WCAG AA; GDS now monitors against WCAG 2.2.

questions.q: What alt text should a purely decorative image have?
questions.explain: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip it.

questions.q: What do the WCAG principles POUR stand for?
questions.explain: They're the four principles behind every WCAG success criterion.

questions.q: Why do properly marked-up headings matter for accessibility?
options: Screen reader users navigate by them to understand and move through a page
questions.explain: Heading structure is one of the most used navigation methods for screen reader users.

questions.q: Which of these is the least leading interview question?
options: Don't you find the form confusing?
Tell me about the last time you applied for this
Would you like a better form?
How much do you love the new design?
questions.explain: Open questions about real past behaviour give more reliable insight.

questions.q: What happens in usability testing?
options: Users fill in a satisfaction survey
You watch people try to complete real tasks with a prototype or service
questions.explain: Observing behaviour shows problems people may not report.

questions.q: What does informed consent mean in research?
options: Participants sign anything you give them
Participants understand what's involved, how their data is used, and that they can withdraw
Consent isn't needed for short sessions
questions.explain: It's an ethical and legal foundation of research.

questions.q: What is affinity mapping used for?
options: Grouping research observations to find patterns and themes
questions.explain: It's a common synthesis technique.

questions.q: What is qualitative research best at answering?
options: Why and how people behave as they do
questions.explain: Quantitative research answers how many; qualitative explains why.

questions.q: What does front-loading mean in content design?
options: Putting the most important words at the start of headings, links and sentences
questions.explain: People scan the first few words, so lead with what matters.

questions.q: What reading age does GOV.UK aim to write for, to be understood by most people?
questions.explain: Writing for a reading age of 9 helps everyone, including experts in a hurry.

questions.q: What is pair writing?
options: Two content designers writing different pages
A content designer and a subject expert writing together
questions.explain: It builds shared understanding and speeds up sign-off.

questions.q: What makes good link text?
options: Text that describes where the link goes
questions.explain: Descriptive links help everyone, especially screen reader users who list links out of context.

questions.q: Which is plain English?
questions.explain: The TPXimpact guide says the same: buy, not purchase.

questions.q: What does a service blueprint show that a journey map usually doesn't?
options: The behind-the-scenes people, processes and systems supporting each step
questions.explain: Blueprints connect front-stage experience with back-stage delivery.

questions.q: What is the first point of the GOV.UK Service Standard?
questions.explain: Point 2 is to solve a whole problem for users.

questions.q: Why start with low-fidelity prototypes?
options: They let you test ideas quickly and cheaply before committing
questions.explain: Raise fidelity as confidence grows.

questions.q: What is a journey map?
options: The steps a user goes through over time and their experience at each one
questions.explain: It helps teams see the service from the user's point of view.

questions.q: What does solving a whole problem for users mean?
options: Designing around the user's full task across channels and organisations, not one team's piece
questions.explain: Users don't care about organisational boundaries.

questions.q: What should a good error message do?
options: Say what went wrong and how to fix it, in plain language
questions.explain: The GOV.UK Design System has detailed guidance on error messages.

questions.q: What is a design system?
options: Reusable components and patterns, with guidance on when and how to use them
questions.explain: It keeps services consistent and speeds up delivery.

questions.q: What is progressive disclosure?
options: Showing only what's needed now and revealing more when it's asked for
questions.explain: It reduces cognitive load.

questions.q: What does Fitts's law tell us?
options: Users read in an F pattern
The time to reach a target depends on its size and distance
Seven items is the memory limit
questions.explain: Make important targets bigger and easier to reach.

questions.q: Why does GOV.UK often use a one thing per page pattern?
options: It helps people focus, reduces errors and works well on mobile
questions.explain: It's a well-tested pattern for complex forms.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Give everyone admin rights to save time
Give people and systems only the access they need to do their job
questions.explain: It limits damage if an account is compromised.

questions.q: What's the best defence against SQL injection?
questions.explain: Parameterised queries keep data separate from commands.

questions.q: Multi-factor authentication combines:
options: Two or more different kinds of factor, such as something you know and something you have
questions.explain: Two passwords are the same factor type.

questions.q: Which is in the OWASP Top 10?
questions.explain: Broken access control is at the top of the 2021 list.

questions.q: What protects data while it travels over a network?
questions.explain: Use both encryption in transit and at rest.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of infrastructure as code?
options: Repeatable, version-controlled environments that can be reviewed like code
It removes the need for security
questions.explain: Tools include Terraform, Bicep and CloudFormation.

questions.q: What is horizontal scaling?
options: Adding more CPU to one server
Adding more instances to share the load
questions.explain: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger; horizontal adds more machines.

questions.q: What does recovery time objective (RTO) mean?
options: How much data you can lose
The longest acceptable time to restore a service after an outage
questions.explain: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose.

questions.q: Why deploy across multiple availability zones?
options: So the service survives the failure of one data centre
questions.explain: It's a core resilience pattern.

questions.q: What does terraform plan do?
options: Shows the changes Terraform would make, without making them
questions.explain: Reviewing the plan before apply catches mistakes.

questions.q: What is continuous integration?
options: Merging small changes often, with automated builds and tests on every change
questions.explain: It finds problems early, while they're small.

questions.q: Which HTTP method should be safe and idempotent for reading data?
questions.explain: GET shouldn't change state.

questions.q: What is refactoring?
options: Changing the structure of code without changing its behaviour
questions.explain: Good tests make refactoring safe.

questions.q: In semantic versioning, which part changes for a breaking change?
questions.explain: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking changes bump MAJOR.

questions.q: What is the main value of code review?
options: Sharing knowledge and catching issues early
questions.explain: Reviews spread understanding across the team.

questions.q: What is an architecture decision record (ADR)?
options: A short record of a decision, its context and consequences
questions.explain: ADRs help future teams understand why things are the way they are.

questions.q: What does loose coupling allow?
options: Systems to change and scale independently
questions.explain: Tightly coupled systems force changes to ripple across each other.

questions.q: What should a build-or-buy decision consider beyond the purchase price?
options: Total cost of ownership, fit with user needs, lock-in and skills to run it
questions.explain: The Technology Code of Practice asks teams to consider these.

questions.q: What is TOGAF's Architecture Development Method (ADM)?
options: A method for developing and managing enterprise architecture
questions.explain: It's a cycle from vision through to change management.

questions.q: Which does the Technology Code of Practice encourage?
options: Open standards and making source code open
questions.explain: It also asks teams to use cloud first and make things secure.

questions.q: What's the difference between an incident and a problem?
options: An incident is an unplanned interruption. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents
questions.explain: Incident management restores service; problem management prevents recurrence.

questions.q: What is a service level agreement (SLA)?
options: An agreement on the levels of service a provider will deliver
questions.explain: SLAs set targets such as response and resolution times.

questions.q: What does a configuration management database (CMDB) hold?
options: Configuration items and how they relate to each other
questions.explain: It helps assess the impact of changes and incidents.

questions.q: What does first contact resolution measure?
options: How fast the phone is answered
Requests resolved at the first contact, without escalation
Number of tickets closed per day
questions.explain: It's a strong indicator of service desk effectiveness.

questions.q: Which improvement cycle is widely used in service management?
questions.explain: PDCA underpins continual service improvement.

questions.q: What is an AI hallucination?
options: Output that sounds confident but is wrong or made up
questions.explain: Check facts and sources, especially in client work.

questions.q: What should you do before using a generative AI tool with client data?
options: Paste it in to save time
Check the tool is approved and follow data and security policies, avoiding personal or sensitive data unless allowed
Ask the tool if it's safe
questions.explain: The UK government's AI Playbook stresses this.

questions.q: What does human in the loop mean?
options: People review and can override AI outputs before they're acted on
questions.explain: It's key for high-impact decisions.

questions.q: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) do?
options: Finds relevant documents and gives them to the model to ground its answer
questions.explain: It reduces hallucinations and keeps answers current.

questions.q: Which usually improves a prompt?
options: Giving clear context, the goal, the format you want and examples
Asking several unrelated things at once
questions.explain: Specific prompts get specific results.

questions.q: What are the four stages of Kolb's experiential learning cycle?
options: Concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation
questions.explain: Our consulting skills programme draws on Kolb.

questions.q: How is coaching different from mentoring?
options: Coaching helps someone find their own answers. Mentoring shares the mentor's experience and advice
questions.explain: Both are useful; choose based on what the person needs.

questions.q: What is psychological safety in a team?
options: People feel safe to speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes
questions.explain: It's strongly linked to team learning and performance.

questions.q: Which feedback model structures feedback as situation, behaviour and impact?
questions.explain: It keeps feedback specific and about behaviour, not personality.

questions.q: What's the main benefit of pairing with a client colleague?
options: Transferring skills so the client can carry on after you leave
questions.explain: Leaving clients confident is part of our purpose.

questions.q: What is a theory of change?
options: A description of how activities are expected to lead to outcomes and impact
questions.explain: It makes assumptions explicit so they can be tested.

questions.q: What is a counterfactual?
options: What would have happened without the intervention
questions.explain: Comparing with it shows the real difference made.

questions.q: What is the Magenta Book?
questions.explain: The Green Book covers appraisal; the Magenta Book covers evaluation.

questions.q: What's the difference between process and impact evaluation?
options: Process looks at how it was delivered. Impact looks at what difference it made
questions.explain: Many evaluations combine both.

questions.q: Why capture a baseline?
options: So you can measure change against how things were before
questions.explain: Without a baseline it's hard to show impact.

questions.q: What is span of control?
options: The number of people who report directly to a manager
questions.explain: Very wide or very narrow spans both bring problems.

questions.q: What does an operating model describe?
options: How an organisation delivers value: its people, processes, technology, structure and governance
questions.explain: Org design often starts from the target operating model.

questions.q: What is Conway's law?
options: Systems tend to mirror the communication structures of the organisations that build them
questions.explain: It's why org design and technology design are linked.

questions.q: In a matrix structure, people typically:
options: Report along two lines, such as practice and project
questions.explain: Consultancies like ours often work this way.

questions.q: Which model looks at strategy, structure, processes, rewards and people together?
questions.explain: Changing one point affects the others.

questions.q: What does MECE mean in structured problem solving?
questions.explain: Breaking problems down with no overlaps and no gaps.

questions.q: In a power and interest stakeholder grid, how should you treat high power, high interest stakeholders?
questions.explain: Engage them actively and often.

questions.q: What is a BATNA in negotiation?
options: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement
questions.explain: Knowing it tells you when to walk away.

questions.q: What is the pyramid principle in communication?
options: Start with the detail and build to the answer
Lead with the main message, then the supporting arguments and evidence
questions.explain: Senior audiences want the answer first.

questions.q: What's a facilitator's main job in a workshop?
options: Designing and guiding the process so the group reaches good outcomes together
questions.explain: Good facilitation is mostly preparation.
